title: API 510 Training in Lake Charles: Online Vessel Exam Prep
description: Self-paced API 510 exam prep for Lake Charles and Westlake vessel inspectors: refinery columns, cracker drums, chlor-alkali and LNG pretreatment vessels.
h1: API 510 Training in Lake Charles: Pressure Vessel Inspector Exam Prep for Westlake Refineries, Olefins and Chlor-Alkali Plants and LNG Terminals
html:
API 510 exam prep for pressure vessel inspectors in Lake Charles and Westlake

Cross the Calcasieu River from downtown Lake Charles and the skyline turns into process equipment: crude and vacuum towers, coke drums, cracker quench towers, caustic evaporators and, further south toward Hackberry, the amine contactors and dehydration beds of the LNG export terminals. Every one of those vessels sits in somebody's inspection plan, and Calcasieu Parish inspection groups want the person who signs that plan to hold API 510. This page is for NDT technicians who take the readings, plant inspectors without the certificate, engineers moving into integrity roles, and welders and fitters who repair vessels at turnarounds.

There is no Atlantis classroom in Lake Charles. The API 510 course is self-paced and online, and an instructor answers your questions as you study, so a candidate in Sulphur, Moss Bluff or a rotation camp near Hackberry can prepare without taking leave. The American Petroleum Institute decides who is eligible, administers the examination at Prometric test centres and issues the certification. Finishing the course gets you ready for that examination; it is not a certificate, and Atlantis is not an API-approved training provider.

Refinery vessels on the Westlake side of the river

The U.S. Energy Information Administration's refinery capacity survey for January 2026 lists three refining sites around Lake Charles and Westlake worth knowing unit by unit, alongside a large refinery in Sulphur. Crude distillation is in barrels per calendar day and the other units in barrels per stream day.

Site (EIA listing)Units listedVessel families behind those units
Phillips 66, WestlakeCrude 263,700; vacuum 128,900; delayed coking 66,543; catalytic cracking 50,941; catalytic reforming 49,086Atmospheric and vacuum towers, coke drums and the coker fractionator, the FCC reactor and regenerator, reformer reactors and their separators
Calcasieu Refining, Lake CharlesCrude 135,500; vacuum 36,000; no cracking, coking or reforming listedCrude and vacuum columns, desalters, overhead accumulators and a large population of exchanger shells
Excel Paralubes, WestlakeGas oil hydrocracking 43,000; no crude unitHydrocracker reactors, high- and low-pressure separators and fractionation vessels in hydrogen service

The Phillips 66 refinery has run since 1941 on roughly 690 acres beside the river, and besides its delayed coker it has a specialty coker and calciner making graphite petroleum coke for the steel industry. Coke drums heat, fill and quench every cycle, a reminder that service, not just corrosion, can decide an interval. Louisiana's 2025 refinery report says Excel Paralubes began in 1994 as a lube hydrocracker and takes vacuum gas oil from the Phillips 66 refinery next door, sending lighter distillate back, so two sites' vessels share one feed. The report calls Calcasieu Refining an independent refiner; a plant with no conversion units still has towers, drums and exchangers enough to keep inspectors busy, and its crude slate decides which hot-section mechanisms matter.

Crackers, chlor-alkali and vinyls: vessels beyond the refineries

LyondellBasell and Sasol own a 1.5 million-ton ethane cracker and 0.9 million tons a year of low-density and linear low-density polyethylene capacity in a 50/50 joint venture that LyondellBasell operates, and Sasol still describes Lake Charles as its most significant site in the United States. A cracker brings quench water towers, caustic wash towers, compressor suction drums and a cold fractionation train of deethanizers, depropanizers and splitters, each with its own design temperature and failure mode.

Westlake operates a large ethylene complex near Lake Charles, and GlobalData's profile of the complex lists ethylene, chlorine, caustic soda, ethylene dichloride and vinyl chloride monomer among its products. In December 2025 Westlake shut three Lake Charles assets: the vinyl chloride monomer plant at Lake Charles North, one diaphragm chlor-alkali unit at Lake Charles South and the styrene plant. A closure is paperwork as well as steel, because someone must decide which vessels are preserved for a possible restart, which are decommissioned and which records travel with each. The chlor-alkali units still running keep their caustic evaporators and brine and chlorine equipment.

LNG pretreatment vessels south of the city

The Department of Energy's LNG export snapshot for September 2026 lists Cameron LNG at Hackberry with three trains, Venture Global's Calcasieu Pass, operating since March 2022, and Sabine Pass near the Texas line as operating. It shows CP2 in Cameron Parish and Louisiana LNG Infrastructure in Calcasieu Parish under construction, with operations estimated for 2027 and 2029, and Commonwealth in Cameron Parish under construction for 2030. Energy Transfer suspended development of its Lake Charles LNG export project in December 2025.

API 510 work at those plants sits upstream of liquefaction and around the refrigerant systems: inlet separators, amine contactors and regenerators for acid gas removal, molecular sieve dehydrators that cycle hot and cold every regeneration, mercury guard beds and refrigerant drums. The current Body of Knowledge excludes cryogenic vessels below −50°F (−45°C), so the coldest liquefaction equipment is outside the examination while the pretreatment train is inside it. New trains also show why baseline data matters: the first thickness survey after start-up is the reading every later corrosion rate is measured from.

Who answers for a vessel in Calcasieu Parish

Louisiana's boiler and pressure vessel rules, administered by the Office of State Fire Marshal, say they are not designed to provide an inspection program for unfired pressure vessels, except as the state act provides, and that inspections will be made when an owner or user asks. In practice the in-service inspection of a Westlake column or a Hackberry contactor is the owner's programme.

Federal rules frame that programme. OSHA's process safety management standard, which federal OSHA enforces in Louisiana, names pressure vessels in its mechanical integrity paragraph and expects inspection and testing to follow recognized and generally accepted good engineering practices, more often than usual if operating experience indicates. API 510 is the practice most owner-users adopt for vessels, and it defines the authorized pressure vessel inspector and the owner-user inspection organization that employs one, which is why parish job postings ask for the certification. The guide to the owner-user inspection organization explains how those departments work.

Pipelines add a twist. Under 49 CFR 195.432(c), steel aboveground breakout tanks built to API Std 2510, meaning pressurized liquefied gas storage at a hazardous liquid pipeline facility, are inspected according to section 6 of API 510, so a pipeline company's spheres and bullets can be API 510 work too.

The API 510 damage mechanism list, read from Lake Charles

Each window's Body of Knowledge names the API RP 571 mechanisms that can be examined. Most on the current list have a home within a short drive of the Interstate 10 bridge:

  • Hydrochloric acid corrosion. Crude tower overheads where chloride salts hydrolyse, and chlorinated chemistry wherever moisture meets hydrogen chloride.
  • Caustic corrosion and caustic stress corrosion cracking. Caustic evaporators at the chlor-alkali plants and caustic wash towers at the crackers, where concentration, metal temperature and stress relief of the welds decide the risk.
  • Sulfidation and naphthenic acid corrosion. Hot sections and bottoms circuits of crude and vacuum columns, depending on the crude run and the alloy in place.
  • High-temperature H2/H2S corrosion and high temperature hydrogen attack. Hydrocracker and hydrotreater reactors and hot separators.
  • Wet H2S damage and amine stress corrosion cracking. Coker and FCC gas plants, sour water strippers, amine regenerators and the acid gas removal units at the terminals.
  • Erosion. FCC reactors, regenerators and cyclones.
  • Corrosion under insulation and chloride cracking. National Weather Service normals for 1981 to 2010 give Lake Charles Regional Airport 57.49 inches of rain a year, and insulated carbon steel between roughly 10°F and 350°F, or austenitic stainless steel between roughly 140°F and 400°F, counts as susceptible.
  • Brittle fracture. Light-ends vessels that can auto-refrigerate when depressurised.
  • Boiler water and steam condensate corrosion. Deaerators and condensate drums wherever steam is raised.

The examination never asks which plant has which problem; it describes a mechanism, asks which method RP 571 and RP 572 associate with it, and applies API 510's rules to the findings.

Worked example: a sphere, its liquid head and the interval it earns

Spheres for light hydrocarbons such as propylene and LPG are standard at olefins plants and pipeline terminals, and the Body of Knowledge lists the spherical shell formula of ASME Section VIII Division 1, UG-27(d), among the examined calculations. It also states that static head on the examination always uses a specific gravity of 1.0, which happens to be the load a sphere carries during its hydrostatic test.

  • The vessel. Inside diameter 50 ft, so the inside radius R is 300 in.; 180 psi at the top; allowable stress S of 20,000 psi given in the problem; joint efficiency E of 1.0 for a fully radiographed sphere.
  • Static head at the bottom. 0.433 psi per foot × 50 ft = 21.65 psi, so the bottom sees 201.65 psi.
  • Required thickness at the bottom. t = PR ÷ (2SE − 0.2P) = 201.65 × 300 ÷ (40,000 − 40.33) = 60,495 ÷ 39,960 = 1.514 in. At the top, 180 psi gives 1.351 in.
  • Corrosion rate. The lowest bottom-zone reading fell from 1.660 in. to 1.560 in. in ten years: 0.010 in. per year.
  • Remaining allowance and life. 1.560 − 1.514 = 0.046 in., or about 4.6 years at that rate.
  • Interval. The lesser of half the remaining life and 10 years: about 2.3 years.

Now make the common mistake and use the top pressure for the bottom plates. The required thickness drops to 1.351 in., the remaining allowance grows to 0.209 in., the life to about 21 years and the interval to the 10-year cap: an interval more than four times too long, because the liquid head was left out. Had the remaining life come out under four years, API 510 would have allowed an interval equal to it, up to two years. The API 510 course page works cylindrical shells, heads and test pressure the same way.

Routes into API 510 from Lake Charles jobs

API counts experience from the last 10 years while employed by or under contract with an authorized inspection agency, which includes an owner-user inspection organization, and verifies what you claim.

  • Engineers. McNeese State University's chemical engineering degree is accredited by ABET's Engineering Accreditation Commission, and McNeese also offers mechanical, civil and electrical engineering. A bachelor's degree in engineering or technology needs one year of supervising or performing inspection as API 510 describes it.
  • NDT technicians. A two-year degree or certificate in engineering or technology needs two years in the design, construction, repair, operation or inspection of pressure vessels, one of them in supervision or performance of inspection; a high school diploma needs three. Atlantis's ASNT SNT-TC-1A NDT training in Lake Charles leads into the readings work that builds that record.
  • Process operators. SOWELA Technical Community College in Lake Charles offers a process technology programme for people heading into operator jobs. Operating experience counts toward the total, but every route includes inspection, so operators usually move into an inspection role first, and API decides whether a given credential counts as an engineering or technology qualification.
  • Welders and fitters. Repair and construction experience counts toward the longer routes; some take AWS CWI exam prep in Lake Charles first.
  • Veterans. API credits three or more years of technical military service as it would a bachelor's degree, and two years as a two-year degree; a dishonorable discharge cancels that credit.

Candidates with no formal education need five or more years; the API 510 certification requirements page has the full rules.

Studying API 510 on a Lake Charles schedule, and sitting the exam

Plants here run rotating shifts, inspection departments swell at turnarounds, and the LNG construction sites keep long rotations of their own. A self-paced course bends around that: calculation practice on days off, short open-book drills during a turnaround, API 510's closed-book rules reviewed on the drive in. Pick your window from the API exam schedule and study the editions on its Publications Effectivity Sheet, not the books on the office shelf.

The day is long: 170 questions, 140 scored and 30 unscored pretest items, 110 closed-book and 60 open-book, over 7.5 hours with a short tutorial, 2.75 hours closed-book, a 45-minute lunch and 3.75 hours open-book with the code PDFs on screen. Prometric lists test centres in and around Lake Charles; McNeese State University announced in 2018 that its Office of Testing Services had opened a Prometric Testing Center offering the American Petroleum Institute exam among others, but check Prometric's current list once API accepts your application.

Sponsoring API 510 candidates from a Lake Charles plant or contractor

Owner-users and inspection contractors can enrol several candidates under one quote; fees are quoted on request. Each person still applies to API individually with an experience record the employer will be asked to verify, so check every candidate against API's rules before enrolment. Groups do best with one target window, a certified inspector in the department who explains how the code is applied to that site's vessels, and protected study time in the final weeks before the exam.

faq.q: Is there an API 510 class I can attend in person in Lake Charles?
faq.a: No. Atlantis runs no classroom anywhere, Calcasieu Parish included. The API 510 course is self-paced online study with an instructor who answers your questions, which suits rotating shifts and turnaround call-outs better than a fixed timetable would. Some training companies run classroom seminars in other cities if you prefer a concentrated block away from work, but those mean travel, release from the roster and a pace set for the room.

faq.q: Where can I sit the API 510 exam near Lake Charles?
faq.a: API delivers the examination in person at Prometric test centres, and you schedule a seat once API has accepted your application. McNeese State University said in 2018 that its testing office had become a Prometric site offering the American Petroleum Institute exam among many others. Availability changes, so check Prometric's list of centres in and around Lake Charles for your window before you plan around a date.

faq.q: Are the cryogenic heat exchangers at an LNG terminal on the API 510 exam?
faq.a: No. The current Body of Knowledge excludes cryogenic vessels below −50°F (−45°C), so the coldest liquefaction equipment is outside the examination. The pretreatment side of a terminal is different: amine contactors and regenerators, dehydrators, separators and refrigerant drums are ordinary Section VIII vessels, and the mechanisms they suffer, such as amine cracking, wet H2S damage and corrosion under insulation, are on the list you will be examined on.

faq.q: I have a McNeese engineering degree. How soon can I apply for API 510?
faq.a: With a bachelor's degree in engineering or technology, API asks for one year of experience supervising or performing inspection activities as API 510 describes them, gained in the last 10 years under an authorized inspection agency or owner-user organization. A graduate who joins a plant inspection group can get there quickly if the role genuinely involves inspection. Design or process engineering alone does not meet the one-year requirement.

faq.q: Are pressurised spheres at a pipeline terminal API 510 work?
faq.a: Often, yes. Federal pipeline rules at 49 CFR 195.432(c) require in-service steel aboveground breakout tanks built to API Std 2510, the standard for pressurized liquefied gas storage, to be inspected according to section 6 of API 510. A pipeline operator's spheres and bullets therefore follow the same inspection rules as a refinery's vessels, and inspecting them is work an API 510 candidate can describe on the application.

faq.q: Can an inspection contractor in Sulphur enrol a group of technicians?
faq.a: Yes. A contractor or owner-user can sponsor several candidates under one quote, and fees are quoted on request. Each candidate still applies to API in their own name and books their own exam seat, so check every technician's education and experience against API's rules first. Enrolling people who are a year short of eligibility only frustrates them and wastes the study time.
